We have mass spec: m/z 193.1103 (M+?), likely molecular ion. So molecular weight ~193.11. The formula we guessed C11H15NO2? Let's calculate: C11=132, H15=15, N=14, O2=32 => total 193. So matches. Good.

Carbon NMR peaks: 166.40, 144.78, 132.00, 130.07 (x2), 127.80 (x2), 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23.

Interpretation: 166 ppm suggests carbonyl (ester or amide). 144-130 aromatic carbons. So aromatic ring present. 52,49,43 aliphatic carbons (maybe attached to heteroatoms). 19.23 methyl.

Thus likely aromatic carbonyl compound with amine? Formula C11H15NO2 includes one N, two O. Could be an amide (C=O) attached to aromatic ring, plus maybe an ether? 166 ppm could be amide carbonyl (around 165-175). Aromatic carbons 6 signals (some duplicates). So phenyl ring.

Aliphatic carbons: 52,49,43 maybe CH2 attached to N or O. 19.23 methyl attached to carbon (maybe isopropyl). So maybe N-methyl? Let's think of possible structures: e.g., phenacetyl amine? Phenyl-CO-CH2-CH2-NH-CH3? That would be C10? Let's compute: phenyl (C6H5) + CO (C1O1) + CH2CH2 (C2H4) + NHCH3 (C1H4N) total C10? Actually C6+1+2+1=10. Need C11. Maybe phenyl-CO-CH(CH3)-NH-CH3? That gives extra carbon.

Let's compute formula for N-methyl-2-phenylacetamide: C9? Wait: phenyl (C6H5) + CO (C1O1) + CH2 (C1H2) + NHCH3 (C1H4N) = C9? Actually total C6+1+1+1=9. Not enough.

Our formula C11 suggests maybe phenyl ring (6 C) plus carbonyl carbon (1) =7, leaving 4 carbons aliphatic. Could be a phenoxyacetate? But N present.

Maybe it's an amide of phenylacetic acid with N-methylpropyl? Let's try: phenyl-CH2-CO-NH-CH2-CH3? That would be C6 (ring) + CH2 (1) + CO (1) + NH (0) + CH2 (1) + CH3 (1) =10. Not enough.

Add extra methyl on nitrogen: N-methyl phenylacetyl amine? phenyl-CH2-CO-N(CH3)2? That would be C6 + CH2 + CO + N(CH3)2 (2 carbons) =10? Actually N(CH3)2 adds 2 carbons, total 6+1+1+2=10. Still 10.

Need 11 carbons. Maybe phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH2-NH-CH3 (an amide? Actually that's an ester with amine). But formula includes two O, one N. Could be phenyl acetate with amino group.

Consider structure: 4-methoxybenzamide? That would have OMe (adds 1 carbon) plus carbonyl O, N. Formula C8? Actually anisamide: C8? Let's compute: C6H4 (ring) + OCH3 (C1) + CONH2 (C1 O1 N1) = C8? Wait: ring 6, OCH3 adds 1, carbonyl carbon adds 1 => total 8. Not 11.

Our carbon NMR shows 166 ppm carbonyl, aromatic carbons 6 signals (makes sense for monosubstituted phenyl). Aliphatic carbons: 52,49,43,19. That's four distinct aliphatic carbons. Could be a side chain with hetero atoms.

52 ppm typical for carbon attached to O (e.g., O-CH3 ~55). 49 ppm maybe CH2 attached to N. 43 maybe CH attached to N? 19 methyl.

Thus maybe structure: phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH(NHCH3)-CH3? That's an ester with amine? But we need N present.

Consider phenyl acetate with N-methylamino group: phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH2-NH-CH3. Carbons: phenyl 6, carbonyl 1, O-CH2 1, CH2 1, N-CH3 1 =10. Need one more carbon maybe extra CH3 on nitrogen (dimethyl). So phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH2-N(CH3)2 gives C11. Let's compute: phenyl 6, carbonyl 1, O-CH2 1, CH2 1, two N-CH3 (2) =11. Good. O count: carbonyl O (1) + ester O (1) =2. N count 1. So formula C11H? Let's compute H: phenyl C6H5, carbonyl carbon no H, O-CH2 (CH2) 2 H, CH2 2 H, N(CH3)2 gives 6 H, total H =5+2+2+6=15. Yes matches C11H15NO2. Good!

Now carbon shifts: carbonyl 166 ppm matches ester carbonyl. Aromatic carbons 144-127 range matches phenyl with electron-withdrawing carbonyl (para? but monosubstituted). O-CH2 attached to carbonyl O (ester) typical ~60 ppm, we have 52. Could be slightly lower due to adjacent N? Actually O-CH2 attached to carbonyl O (alkoxy) ~60. 52 is a bit low but plausible for O-CH2 attached to carbonyl and also adjacent to CH2? 49 ppm could be CH2 attached to O and N? Actually CH2 next to O and N maybe ~45-55. 43 ppm could be N-CH3? N-CH3 typical ~30-40. 19 ppm methyl attached to N maybe ~30? Hmm.

But we have two N-CH3? Actually N(CH3)2 gives two equivalent methyls ~30 ppm. But we have only one methyl at 19 ppm, which is lower (alkyl). So maybe not dimethyl.

Alternative: phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH(NHCH3)-CH3 (i.e., ester of lactic acid with phenyl). Carbons: phenyl 6, carbonyl 1, O-CH2 1, CH (bearing NHCH3) 1, CH3 (attached to that carbon) 1, N-CH3 1 =11. Good. H count: phenyl 5, O-CH2 2, CH (1 H), CH3 (3), N-CH3 (3) =14? plus NH (1) =15. Yes matches.

Carbon shifts: O-CH2 ~52, CH attached to N and O (alpha carbon) maybe ~49, N-CH3 ~43, methyl attached to carbon (CH3) ~19. That matches observed: 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23. Good!

Thus structure is phenyl acetate of lactic acid with N-methyl? Actually lactic acid is CH3-CH(OH)-COOH. Here we have O-CH2-CH(NHCH3)-CH3 attached to phenyl carbonyl? Wait we have phenyl-CO-O-CH2-CH(NHCH3)-CH3. That's phenyl ester of N-methyl-2-hydroxypropyl? Actually O-CH2-CH(NHCH3)-CH3 is 2-amino-1-propanol methylated? It's 2-amino-1-propanol with N-methyl.

Thus SMILES: O=C(OCC(CN)C)C1=CC=CC=C1? Need N-methyl: CN attached to CH? Actually CH(NCH3) means N attached to CH, not CH attached to N? The side chain: O-CH2-CH(NCH3)-CH3. So SMILES: O=C(OCC(C)N)C1=CC=CC=C1 with N-methyl? Wait CH(NCH3) means carbon attached to N which has a methyl substituent. So N is attached to carbon and also has a methyl group: -CH(N(CH3))-CH3. So side chain: O-CH2-CH(N(C) )-CH3. SMILES: O=C(OCC(C)N(C)C?) Actually N attached to CH and methyl, but also maybe H? N is tertiary? N(C) attached to carbon and methyl, plus H? N-methyl secondary amine: -CH(NHCH3)-CH3. So N has H and CH3. So side chain: O-CH2-CH(NHCH3)-CH3. SMILES: O=C(OCC(C)N)C1=CC=CC=C1 with N having a methyl: N(C). So O=C(OCC(C)N(C)C?) Wait N(C)C would be dimethyl. Need N(C)H. In SMILES, secondary amine: N(C) means N attached to methyl and implicit H. So CH(N(C))CH3. So side chain: O-CH2-CH(N(C))CH3. So full SMILES: O=C(OCC(C)N(C))c1ccccc1. Let's test formula: Count C: phenyl 6, carbonyl carbon 1, O-CH2 1, CH (1), CH3 (1), N-methyl (1) =11. H: phenyl 5, O-CH2 2, CH (1), CH3 3, N-CH3 3, plus NH (1) =15. O2, N1. Good.

Thus final answer SMILES: O=C(OCC(C)N(C))c1ccccc1

Check validity? Use validate? Let's quickly validate.
